synopsis: South African mining regulations require collision-prevention systems to fail to safe without human intervention; Regulation 8.10 describes warning, retardation toward a safe speed if the operator does not act, and then automatic braking [f1362, f2441]. MOSH specifies fail-to-safe within 500 ms of detecting a critical failure and lost-connection detection within 500 ms, although one HIL comparison lists both 500 ms and 50 ms fail-to-safe limits without explaining their respective scope [f2359, f12076, f5698]. MOSH specifies emergency-stop deceleration of 1.9 m/s² for machines exceeding 20 km/h and 1.0 m/s² for others, versus controlled-stop values of 1.0 or 0.5 m/s²; abrupt or false braking can itself create hazards and reduce acceptance [f5560, f5561, f1536, f3622]. Post-stop safety requires attention to brake hold and release: ISO 21815-3 recommends operator action before release where needed to prevent rollaway, but off-road implementation data was not found [f6305, f6525, f6526]. Human overrides and recovery are material risks: a June 2017 fatal-accident investigation recorded 87 prior emergency-stop overrides, while WorkSafe WA Report 286, dated 7 March 2025, describes autonomous trucks resuming movement after communications restoration while operators approached them [f3295, f10718]. HIL data injection can test timing, diagnostics and fail-to-safe behaviour, but functional safety does not establish perception capability; validation should explicitly cover degraded modes, recovery and post-stop hazards rather than nominal driving alone [f5697, f12021, f10778, f11035, f6600].
